cim: Status and influencing factors of artificial intelligence readiness among nursing students
cim_eredeti: Status and influencing factors of artificial intelligence readiness among nursing students
szoveg_eredeti:
Volume 13 - 2026 | https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.2007016

Department of medicine, Jingchu University of Technology, Jingmen, China

To investigate the current status of artificial intelligence (AI) readiness among nursing students and analyze its influencing factors, providing evidence for the cultivation of AI literacy in nursing education.

A total of 684 nursing students from two universities in Hubei Province were recruited as study participants. Data were collected using a general demographic questionnaire and the Chinese version of the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students (C-MAIRS-MS). Descriptive statistics, univariate analysis, and multiple linear regression analysis were employed for data processing.

The overall mean score of AI readiness among nursing students was 3.47 ± 0.31; the cognitive dimension scored the highest (3.57 ± 0.44), while the competency dimension scored the lowest (3.32 ± 0.48). Multiple linear regression analysis revealed that education level, Self-rated academic performance, Student cadre, Innovation and entrepreneurship project, Large language model use frequency, AI course learning, Programming foundation were significant predictors of AI readiness, collectively explaining 33.3% of the total variance (R2 = 0.333, adjusted R2 = 0.311, F = 15.030, P < 0.001)

Nursing students’ AI readiness remains suboptimal with room for improvement. Targeted interventions addressing key predictors are essential to strengthen AI competency among nursing students.

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technology is profoundly reshaping global healthcare delivery systems, ranging from intelligent diagnostic decision-support systems and nursing robots to electronic health record analytics and remote health monitoring, AI technology has permeated the entire spectrum of disease prevention, clinical diagnosis, rehabilitation nursing, and health management (1). In 2024, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued guidance on the ethics and governance of large multi-modal models for health. This guidance provides an international framework for the standardized use of AI in nursing education and clinical practice (2).

As the core force of the future nursing workforce, nursing students’ AI readiness directly determines the quality of intelligent nursing services and patient safety. Medical AI readiness is defined as healthcare providers’ readiness to effectively employ AI applications. It reflects their ability to integrate AI with professional expertise to deliver clinical services across prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation (3). In 2021, Karaca developed the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students (MAIRS-MS) based on this concept, encompassing four dimensions: cognition, competency, vision, and ethics, providing a reliable instrument for systematically assessing medical students’ AI readiness (3). The scale has subsequently been cross-culturally validated in China (4), Iran (5), Malaysia (6), Saudi Arabia (7), Turkey (8), and Jordan (9), demonstrating excellent psychometric properties and cross-cultural applicability.

In recent years, scholars worldwide have conducted exploratory research on nursing students’ AI readiness. A survey of 227 nursing students found that students generally held a moderately positive attitude, although female students exhibited more negative attitudes toward AI than males (10). In another survey of 304 nursing students in Saudi Arabia, the ethics dimension scored the highest while the vision dimension scored the lowest, and educational level together with perceived AI advantages were found to be significant predictors of readiness (11). A quasi-experimental study in Turkey confirmed that a 14-week AI course intervention significantly improved nursing students’ total MAIRS-MS scores and their scores in the cognition, competency, and vision dimensions (12). Separately, a study of 386 Turkish nursing students revealed that AI readiness was significantly positively correlated with individual innovativeness, and that gender, family structure, income status, and AI training experience were all significant influencing factors (13).

In China, nursing education is undergoing a profound transformation from traditional skill-oriented to human-machine collaborative competency-oriented approaches. In 2024, the Ministry of Education reclassified nursing as a state-controlled specialty, signifying the nation's high regard for the quality of nursing talent cultivation (14). The Education Power Construction Plan Outline (2024–2035) explicitly calls for the deep integration of education with cutting-edge technologies such as AI and virtual reality to construct an intelligent educational ecosystem. However, in the nursing talent cultivation system, the curriculum for nursing informatics remains relatively underdeveloped, with insufficient integration of artificial intelligence technology (15).

This study aims to investigate the current status of AI readiness among nursing students and to analyze differences in AI readiness across students with different characteristics, thereby providing a reference for promoting AI education reform in nursing and formulating targeted strategies to enhance AI readiness.

A convenience sampling method was employed to recruit nursing students from two universities in Hubei Province between April and May 2026.

Inclusion criteria were: (1) full-time nursing students currently enrolled in a degree program; and (2) voluntary participation with informed consent.

Exclusion criteria were: (1) students on leave of absence for more than one semester; and (2) students unable to complete the questionnaire due to personal reasons.

An a priori power analysis was conducted using GPower 3.1.9.2. Based on F tests for linear multiple regression (fixed model, R2 deviation from zero), with a medium effect size (f2 = 0.15), α = 0.05, power (1−β) = 0.95, and 44 predictors(22 demographic variables and 22 scale items), the minimum required total sample size was calculated to be 305. The actual sample size of 684 exceeded this requirement, achieving 95% statistical power and effectively minimizing the risk of Type II error, thereby ensuring the robustness of the findings.

A self-designed questionnaire was developed by the researchers, including demographic characteristics (gender, age, educational level, grade, birthplace, family economic status, monthly living expenses), academic background (admission method, self-rated academic performance, student leadership experience, research and innovation projects, plans for postgraduate entrance examination or “top-up” degree program, internship status), and technical exposure experience (frequency of electronic device use, frequency of large language model use, AI course learning, nursing informatics-related courses, AI lectures, computer certificates or programming foundation, family IT background), comprising a total of 22 items.

The C-MAIRS-MS, translated and validated by Tang et al. (16), was originally developed by Karaca et al. (3).The scale comprises four dimensions: cognition (8 items), competency (8 items), vision (3 items), and ethics (3 items), totaling 22 items. A 5-point Likert scale was used, ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), with a total score range of 22–110. Higher scores indicate greater AI readiness.

In this study, the Cronbach’s α coefficient of the scale was 0.967, and the Cronbach’s α coefficients for each dimension were 0.920 (cognition), 0.929 (competency), 0.874 (vision), and 0.878 (ethics), indicating good reliability.
